summary: Describes the file format used to store facsimile (fax) images from the Rapicom 450 fax machine. It is a memo aimed at people who needed to handle that machine's data on their own computers.

eli5.summary: A fax machine turns a picture into a stream of numbers. This memo explains how one particular fax machine writes those numbers into a file so other computers can read them.

questions: how was fax data stored in early networks
subtitle: How a specific fax machine encoded image data into computer files.

tldr.problem: Organizations with Rapicom 450 fax machines needed a way to store and exchange fax images in a standard computer file format.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents the record structure that wraps the fax machine's 585-bit encoded blocks into bytes: a length byte, a command byte, and the data, with specific commands for setup blocks, data blocks, and end-of-file markers.
tldr.outcome: Organizations with compatible fax equipment could exchange fax files reliably. The format is specific to this hardware and depends on understanding the machine's proprietary encoding.

facts.label: Record structure
facts.value: length byte + command byte + data bytes

today: RFC 769 documents a format specific to the Rapicom 450 fax machine. As that hardware became obsolete, the format is now of historical interest only.

sections.title: Fax File Storage
sections.content: Several organizations connected Rapicom 450 facsimile machines to computers so they could store fax images in files and retrieve them later. This memo documents the file format they adopted, so that other organizations with the same fax equipment could exchange these files reliably.
sections.eli5: A fax machine turns a picture into numbers. This memo says how to write those numbers into a file.

sections.title: The Record Format
sections.content:
The Rapicom 450 produces 585-bit data blocks. Each block is stored in a record of 8-bit bytes: a length byte (including itself and the command byte), a command byte, and the data bytes. The length value includes both the length and command bytes, so a record with a 585-bit data block is 76 bytes long (one length, one command, 73.125 rounded to 74 data bytes).

Three command codes are defined: 56 (octal 70) for a setup block, 57 (octal 71) for a data block, and 58 (octal 72) for an end-of-file marker.
sections.eli5: Each piece of the picture gets wrapped in a labeled package: a number saying how big it is, a code saying what kind of data it is, and the picture data itself.

sections.title: File Organization
sections.content:
A complete fax image file always starts with a setup block (the fax machine's configuration), followed by one or more data blocks (the actual scanned image), and ends with an end-of-file record. The first 24 bits of each data block are always a synchronization mark with the value 271141344 in octal. The next two bits of the byte after the sync mark contain a sequence number that cycles 11, 01, 10, 00 across the data records.

The 585-bit data is encoded by the Rapicom 450 hardware, so it cannot be used as a simple bitmap without understanding the machine's proprietary encoding and decoding procedure.
sections.eli5: A fax file is like a deck of labeled cards: first comes the setup card, then picture cards in order, then a done card at the end.
